questions.stem: How did Kelly Swisher feel when she first came across the rat snake?

explain.定位:
But the woman says the snake she encountered Thursday terrified her out of her wits.
但这位女士说，她周四遇到的那条蛇把她吓得魂飞魄散。
explain.信号:
转折 But 后接强情绪词。前句 Rat snakes aren't poisonous or a threat to people
generally. 先说鼠蛇一般无害，But the woman says…terrified her out of her wits 用 But
一转，落到当事人的真实感受上，转折后的这句才是答案句；terrified（吓坏）就是那个情
绪信号词。
explain.替换:
terrified her out of her wits ↔ Scared.
强义到普通义的同义替换
explain.排除:
A) 未提及
Annoyed. 是‘恼火、被惹烦’，录音表达的是被 terrified 吓坏的强烈恐惧，不是嫌烦，情绪
种类与烈度都对不上。
C) 未提及
Confused. 是‘困惑、没搞懂’，录音通篇是被吓坏，没有任何表示她迷惑不解的内容。
D) 未提及
Offended. 是‘被冒犯’，用于人与人之间的言行冒犯，与被一条蛇吓到的场景不搭，录音也
无此意。

"It was rough, with big scales," said Swisher, who was on her way to pick up her friend at the

‘它摸上去很粗糙，有大鳞片，’斯威舍说，事情发生时她正开车去机场接朋友。

直接描述，big scales（大鳞片）正对应选项里关于外观的那一项，是承载答案的细节句。

with big scales ↔ It was covered with large scales.

C) 与原文相反
It was killed by the police on the spot. 说蛇被警察当场打死，但录音结局是
Washington County animal control officers came and captured the snake——动物管
理人员把蛇‘抓走’而非打死，且来的是 animal control officers 不是 police。

Questions 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1 Fast food, it turns out, isn't quite as fast as it used to be. A new study finds that McDonald's posted
its slowest drive-through times since this survey was first conducted fifteen years ago. At McDonald's,
customers will spend on average three minutes and nine seconds from the time they placed their orders
until they received their food. That's about ten seconds more than the industry average—and a lot slower
than a decade ago, according to the study, which was commissioned by QSR, an industry trade
publication. And McDonald's wasn't alone in slowing down: Other chains also saw their drive-through
performance slow down. Among the reasons for the slower service, today there are more choices on the
menu, and the products themselves are more complex and take longer to prepare. Speed, of course, is
essential to the drive-through experience. And drive-throughs are hugely important to chains, such as
McDonald's, Burger King and Taco Bell. "Usually the drive-through accounts for sixty to seventy percent
of all business that goes through a fast-food restaurant," notes Sam Ochers, editor of QSR. Of course,
consumers also want their orders prepared correctly and on that score, Ochers says, "accuracy is still
really high."
事实证明，快餐并不像过去那么快了。一项新研究发现，McDonald's 公布了自该调查首次开展十五年来
最慢的得来速时间。在 McDonald's，顾客从下单到拿到食物平均需要花费三分钟九秒。根据这项由行业
贸易出版物 QSR 委托进行的研究，这比行业平均水平慢了约十秒，也比十年前慢了很多。而且
McDonald's 并非唯一变慢的：其他连锁店的得来速表现也有所放缓。服务变慢的原因包括，如今菜单上
有更多选择，产品本身更复杂，需要更长时间准备。当然，速度对于得来速体验至关重要。而得来速对于
McDonald's、Burger King 和 Taco Bell 等连锁店来说极为重要。QSR 编辑 Sam Ochers 指出："通常
得来速占快餐店所有业务的百分之六十到七十。"当然，消费者也希望订单准确无误，而在这一点上，
Ochers 表示，"准确率仍然非常高。"

questions.stem: What is the news report mainly about?
options: A) A study of the fast-food service.
D) Competition in the fast-food industry.

explain.定位:
Fast food, it turns out, isn't quite as fast as it used to be. A new study finds that McDonald's
posted its slowest drive-through times since this survey was first conducted fifteen years ago.
事实表明，快餐已经没有过去那么快了。一项新研究发现，麦当劳的得来速（汽车餐厅）取
餐时间创下了这项调查十五年前首次开展以来的最慢纪录。
explain.信号:
新闻开头点题句 + a study finds 引出调查。新闻的主旨几乎都砸在第一两句。这里开篇
Fast food, it turns out, isn't quite as fast as it used to be 先抛主题（快餐变慢），紧接
A new study finds that 点明这是一项研究/调查的发现——"开头点题"加"a study
finds"双重信号，锁定主旨在此。
explain.替换:
A new study finds that McDonald's posted its slowest drive-through times ↔
A study of the fast-food service.
drive-through times 概括成 fast-food service
explain.排除:
C) 原词陷阱
C 选项里的 McDonald's 在录音里反复出现（McDonald's posted its slowest drive-
through times），最容易让人"听到品牌就选"。但报道讲的是麦当劳服务"变慢"这一现象
与研究结果，从头到尾没有提任何 new business strategies（新经营策略），属于借品牌
原词偷换主题。
借用原文：A new study finds that McDonald's posted its slowest drive-through times
B) 答非所问
录音结尾确实提到顾客希望订单准确、accuracy is still really high，容易让人联想到"顾客
满意度"。但这只是文末一笔带过的细节，全篇主线是"速度变慢"，customer satisfaction
既非主旨、也不是录音的原话概括，属于拿一个尾部细节冒充全篇主题。
借用原文：accuracy is still really high
D) 未提及
D 用了贯穿全篇的 fast-food（goes through a fast-food restaurant）这一原词，看着很
贴。但 competition（竞争）一词在录音里根本没出现，报道讲的是各家"速度都变慢了"，
是横向现象，不是品牌间的竞争较量，属于借原词无中生有。
借用原文：goes through a fast-food restaurant

questions.stem: What has slowed down McDonald's drive-through service?
options: D) The rising number of customers.

explain.定位:
Among the reasons for the slower service, today there are more choices on the menu, and the
products themselves are more complex and take longer to prepare.
在导致服务变慢的诸多原因中，如今菜单上的选择更多了，而且产品本身更复杂、准备起来
要花更长时间。
explain.信号:
原因信号 among the reasons 后紧跟答案。听力定位原因靠信号词，不靠通篇扫描。这里
Among the reasons for the slower service（在变慢的诸多原因中）是一个明牌的原因引
导句，它后面紧跟的 more choices on the menu 和 products themselves are more
complex and take longer to prepare 就是原因本体，锁定在此。
explain.替换:
more choices on the menu ↔ Increased variety of products.
more choices on the menu = increased variety of products
the products themselves are more complex and take longer to prepare ↔
Increased variety of products.
产品更复杂、要更久 与 种类增多 同指一处原因
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
A 的 Customers 是录音里的高频原词（consumers also want their orders prepared
correctly），听到 customers 很想选。但录音只说顾客"希望订单做对"，从没说顾客"要求
更高（higher demands）"，更没把它列为变慢的原因，属于借 customers 原词偷换成另
一个未提的归因。
借用原文：consumers also want their orders prepared correctly
B) 未提及
B 把变慢归咎于 employees 效率低，但录音从头到尾没有出现 employees、也没说任
何"员工慢/效率低"的内容。它靠的是常识联想（人手慢导致排队慢），而非原文依据，是凭
母语常识脑补出来的原因。
D) 张冠李戴
D 的 customers 同样是原词（consumers also want their orders prepared
correctly），且"顾客增多导致变慢"听着很顺。但录音给出的变慢原因是"菜单选择多、产
品更复杂"，根本没提顾客数量上升（rising number），D 把一个录音未说的原因安在"变
慢"头上，属盗用原词后的张冠李戴。
借用原文：consumers also want their orders prepared correctly

questions.stem: What is the news report mainly about?
options: A) International treaties regarding space travel programs.
B) Legal issues involved in commercial space exploration.
C) U.S. government's approval of private space missions.
D) Competition among public and private space companies.

explain.定位:
U.S. government officials are set to approve a mission by privately-held space company
Moon Express to travel outside of Earth's orbit in late 2017.
美国政府官员即将批准私营航天公司 Moon Express 在 2017 年底执行一项飞出地球轨道的
任务。
explain.信号:
新闻第二句总起即落点。新闻报道的主旨几乎总在开头给出。第一句 The first private
mission outside of Earth's orbit is closer than many of us think. 抛出话题，紧接的第二
句 U.S. government officials are set to approve a mission by privately-held space
company Moon Express 把"政府批准私营登月任务"这一核心事件交代清楚，这就是全文
落点。
explain.替换:
U.S. government officials are set to approve a mission ↔
U.S. government's approval of private space missions
动词转名词的同义改写
privately-held space company Moon Express ↔ private space missions
同根词替换
explain.排除:
A) 原词陷阱
录音确实念到 Under international treaties（国际条约），A 就把 International treaties
端出来诱你"听到就选"。但条约只是文中解释"为何此事法律复杂"的一个背景细节，绝非全
文主旨，拿它当主旨是以偏概全。
借用原文：Under international treaties, the U.S. is responsible for the cargo of both public and
private spacecraft.
B) 原词陷阱
录音里有 This makes commercial space travel a complex legal issue，B 便把 Legal
issues involved in commercial space exploration. 摆出来。但"法律问题复杂"只是文中由
条约引出的一句补充说明，整条新闻讲的是"获批"这件事，把一句补充说明拔高为主旨属以
偏概全。
借用原文：This makes commercial space travel a complex legal issue not just domestically,
but abroad.
D) 过度推断
录音结尾提到 Moon Express is not the only company seeking the rights to travel to
outer space. 并带出 SpaceX，D 便顺势说 Competition among public and private
space companies.。但原文只是"补充还有别家公司也在做"，从未说它们在"竞
争/competition"，这是凭只言片语过度推断。
借用原文：Moon Express is not the only company seeking the rights to travel to outer space.

questions.stem: What is Moon Express planning to do?
options: A) Deliver scientific equipment to the moon.
B) Approve a new mission to travel into outer space.
C) Work with federal agencies on space programs.
D) Launch a manned spacecraft to Mars.

explain.定位:
Moon Express's mission involves plans to land a suitcase-sized package of scientific
equipment on the moon for ongoing exploration and commercial development.
Moon Express 的任务包含一项计划：把一个手提箱大小、装有科学设备的包裹送上月球，
用于持续的探索和商业开发。
explain.信号:
主语 Moon Express + plans 引出动作。定位靠"主体名 + 计划信号词"：这句以 Moon
Express's mission involves plans to 开头，主语正是题目要问的 Moon Express，plans
to 直接引出它要做的动作 land a suitcase-sized package of scientific equipment on
the moon，答案就在这里。
explain.替换:
land a suitcase-sized package of scientific equipment on the moon ↔
Deliver scientific equipment to the moon
动词同义 + 细节略写
explain.排除:
B) 张冠李戴
录音里 U.S. government officials are set to approve a mission 的 approve 和 mission
都念到了，B 便拼成 Approve a new mission to travel into outer space.。可"批准任
务"是美国政府的动作，不是 Moon Express 的——后者是"被批准"的一方。把政府的动作
安到 Moon Express 头上，是张冠李戴。
借用原文：U.S. government officials are set to approve a mission
C) 偷换概念
录音念到 coordinated conversations between a number of federal agencies，C 便造
出 Work with federal agencies on space programs.。但原文 federal agencies 是在描
述"获批前各联邦机构之间的沟通协调"这个过程，并没有说 Moon Express 要"与联邦机构
合作（work with）开展项目"，把背景过程偷换成 Moon Express 的计划。
借用原文：The decision involved months of lobbying and coordinated conversations between a
number of federal agencies.
D) 张冠李戴
录音结尾 Elon Musk's SpaceX aims to send an unmanned aircraft to Mars by 2018 提
到了 Mars，D 便端出 Launch a manned spacecraft to Mars.。但去火星的是 SpaceX、
不是 Moon Express；而且原文是 unmanned（无人），选项却写 manned（载人），既
张冠李戴又改了细节，双重错。
借用原文：Elon Musk's SpaceX aims to send an unmanned aircraft to Mars by 2018.

questions.stem: What does Moon Express think of its mission?

explain.定位:
A Moon Express representative declined to comment on the story but noted that the company
is very optimistic about its proposal.
Moon Express 的一位代表拒绝就此事置评，但指出公司对自己的提案非常乐观。
explain.信号:
转折 but 后才是真态度。这句前半 declined to comment（拒绝置评）是烟雾弹，真正的
态度在转折词 but 之后：but noted that the company is very optimistic about its
proposal，very optimistic（非常乐观）就是 Moon Express 的明确表态。听力里 but 之
后才是落点。
explain.替换:
the company is very optimistic about its proposal ↔ It is promising.
乐观与看好的同义对应
explain.排除:
A) 偷换概念
It is significant.（重大/意义重大）虽同为正面词，但原文 very optimistic 说的是"看好前
景"，并没有说任务"意义重大"。significant 谈的是"重要性"，optimistic/promising 谈的
是"前景乐观"，两个维度不同，属在同色彩里偷换评价维度。
借用原文：the company is very optimistic about its proposal
C) 与原文相反
It is unpredictable.（难以预料）是不确定、偏负面的态度，而原文 very optimistic 是明
确的乐观看好，极性正好相反。把"乐观"听成"难料"是方向性错误。
借用原文：the company is very optimistic about its proposal
D) 与原文相反
It is unprofitable.（无利可图）是负面评价，与原文 very optimistic 的乐观看好完全相
悖；况且 optimistic about its proposal 恰恰暗示看好其（含商业）前景，谈不上无利可
图。
借用原文：the company is very optimistic about its proposal

questions.passage:
As Tourists Crowd Out Locals, Venice Faces 'Endangered' List

A) On a recent fall morning, a large crowd blocked the steps at one of Venice's main tourist sites, the Rialto Bridge. The Rialto Bridge is one of the four bridges spanning the Grand Canal. It is the oldest bridge across the canal, and was the dividing line between the districts of San Marco and San Polo. But on this day, there was a twist: it was filled with Venetians, not tourists.

B) "People are cheering and holding their carts in the air," says Giovanni Giorgio, who helped organize the march with a grass-roots organization called Generazione '90. The carts he refers to are small shopping carts—the symbol of a true Venetian. "It started as a joke," he says with a laugh. "The idea was to put blades on the wheels! You know? Like Ben Hur. Precisely like that, you just go around and run people down."

C) Venice is one of the hottest tourist destinations in the world. But that's a problem. Up to 90,000 tourists crowd its streets and canals every day—far outnumbering the 55,000 permanent residents. The tourist increase is one key reason the city's population is down from 175,000 in the 1950s. The outnumbered Venetians have been steadily fleeing. And those who stick around are tired of living in a place where they can't even get to the market without swimming through a sea of picture-snapping tourists. Imagine, navigating through 50,000 people while on the way to school or to work.

D) Laura Chigi, a grandmother at the march, says the local and national governments have failed to do anything about the crowds for decades, because they're only interested in tourism—the primary industry in Venice, worth more than $3 billion in 2015. "Venice is a cash cow," she says, "and everyone wants a piece."

E) Just beyond St. Mark's Square, a cruise ship passes, one of hundreds every year that appear over their medieval(中世纪的) surroundings. Their massive wake creates waves at the bottom of the sea, weakening the foundations of the centuries-old buildings themselves. "Every time I see a cruise ship, I feel sad," Chigi says. "You see the mud it drags; the destruction it leaves in its wake? That hurts the ancient wooden poles holding up the city underwater. One day we'll see Venice break down."

F) For a time, UNESCO, the cultural wing of the United Nations, seemed to agree. Two years ago, it put Italy on notice, saying the government was not protecting Venice. UNESCO considers the entire city a World Heritage Site, a great honor that means Venice, at the cultural level, belongs to all of the world's people. In 2014, UNESCO gave Italy two years to manage Venice's flourishing tourism or the city would be placed on another list—World Heritage In Danger, joining such sites as Aleppo and Palmyra, destroyed by the war in Syria.

G) Venice's deadline passed with barely a murmur(嘟哝) this summer, just as UNESCO was meeting in Istanbul. Only one representative, Jad Tabet from Lebanon, tried to raise the issue. "For several years, the situation of heritage in Venice has been worsening, and it has now reached a dramatic situation," Tabet told UNESCO. "We have to act quickly—there is not a moment to waste."

H) But UNESCO didn't even hold a vote. "It's been postponed until 2017," says Anna Somers, the founder and CEO of The Art Newspaper and the former head of Venice in Peril, a group devoted to restoring Venetian art. She says the main reason the U.N. cultural organization didn't vote to declare Venice a World Heritage Site In Danger is because UNESCO has become "intensely politicized. There would have been some back-room negotiations."

I) Italy boasts more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country in the world, granting it considerable power and influence within the organization. The former head of the UNESCO World Heritage Centre, which oversees heritage sites, is Francesco Bandarin, a Venetian who now serves as UNESCO's assistant director-general for culture.

J) Earlier this year, Italy signed an accord with UNESCO to establish a task force of police art detectives and archaeologists(考古学家) to protect cultural heritage from natural disasters and terror groups, such as ISIS. The accord underlined Italy's global reputation as a good steward of art and culture.

K) But adding Venice to the UNESCO endangered list—which is dominated by sites in developing and conflict-ridden countries—would be an international embarrassment, and could even hurt Italy's profitable tourism industry. The Italian Culture Ministry says it is unaware of any government efforts to pressure UNESCO. As for the organization itself, it declined a request for an interview.

L) The city's current mayor, Luigi Brugnaro, has ridiculed UNESCO and told it to mind its own business, while continuing to support the cruise ship industry, which employs 5,000 Venice residents.

M) As for Venetians, they're beyond frustrated and hoping for a solution soon. "It's a nightmare for me. Some situations are really difficult with tourists around," says Giorgio as he navigates around a swelling crowd at the Rialto Bridge. "There are just so many of them. They never know where they are going, and do not walk in an orderly manner. Navigating the streets can be exhausting."

N) Then it hits him: This crowd isn't made up of tourists. They're Venetians. Giorgio says he's never experienced the Rialto Bridge this way in all his 22 years. "For once, we are the ones who are blocking the traffic," he says delightedly. "It feels unreal. It feels like we're some form of endangered species. It's just nice. The feeling is just pure." But, he worries, if tourism isn't managed and his fellow locals continue to move to the mainland, his generation might be the last who can call themselves native Venetians.

questions.stem: If tourism gets out of control, native Venetians may desert the city altogether one day.
questions.passage:
As Tourists Crowd Out Locals, Venice Faces 'Endangered' List

A) On a recent fall morning, a large crowd blocked the steps at one of Venice's main tourist sites, the Rialto Bridge. The Rialto Bridge is one of the four bridges spanning the Grand Canal. It is the oldest bridge across the canal, and was the dividing line between the districts of San Marco and San Polo. But on this day, there was a twist: it was filled with Venetians, not tourists.

B) "People are cheering and holding their carts in the air," says Giovanni Giorgio, who helped organize the march with a grass-roots organization called Generazione '90. The carts he refers to are small shopping carts—the symbol of a true Venetian. "It started as a joke," he says with a laugh. "The idea was to put blades on the wheels! You know? Like Ben Hur. Precisely like that, you just go around and run people down."

C) Venice is one of the hottest tourist destinations in the world. But that's a problem. Up to 90,000 tourists crowd its streets and canals every day—far outnumbering the 55,000 permanent residents. The tourist increase is one key reason the city's population is down from 175,000 in the 1950s. The outnumbered Venetians have been steadily fleeing. And those who stick around are tired of living in a place where they can't even get to the market without swimming through a sea of picture-snapping tourists. Imagine, navigating through 50,000 people while on the way to school or to work.

D) Laura Chigi, a grandmother at the march, says the local and national governments have failed to do anything about the crowds for decades, because they're only interested in tourism—the primary industry in Venice, worth more than $3 billion in 2015. "Venice is a cash cow," she says, "and everyone wants a piece."

E) Just beyond St. Mark's Square, a cruise ship passes, one of hundreds every year that appear over their medieval(中世纪的) surroundings. Their massive wake creates waves at the bottom of the sea, weakening the foundations of the centuries-old buildings themselves. "Every time I see a cruise ship, I feel sad," Chigi says. "You see the mud it drags; the destruction it leaves in its wake? That hurts the ancient wooden poles holding up the city underwater. One day we'll see Venice break down."

F) For a time, UNESCO, the cultural wing of the United Nations, seemed to agree. Two years ago, it put Italy on notice, saying the government was not protecting Venice. UNESCO considers the entire city a World Heritage Site, a great honor that means Venice, at the cultural level, belongs to all of the world's people. In 2014, UNESCO gave Italy two years to manage Venice's flourishing tourism or the city would be placed on another list—World Heritage In Danger, joining such sites as Aleppo and Palmyra, destroyed by the war in Syria.

G) Venice's deadline passed with barely a murmur(嘟哝) this summer, just as UNESCO was meeting in Istanbul. Only one representative, Jad Tabet from Lebanon, tried to raise the issue. "For several years, the situation of heritage in Venice has been worsening, and it has now reached a dramatic situation," Tabet told UNESCO. "We have to act quickly—there is not a moment to waste."

H) But UNESCO didn't even hold a vote. "It's been postponed until 2017," says Anna Somers, the founder and CEO of The Art Newspaper and the former head of Venice in Peril, a group devoted to restoring Venetian art. She says the main reason the U.N. cultural organization didn't vote to declare Venice a World Heritage Site In Danger is because UNESCO has become "intensely politicized. There would have been some back-room negotiations."

I) Italy boasts more UNESCO World Heritage Sites than any other country in the world, granting it considerable power and influence within the organization. The former head of the UNESCO World Heritage Centre, which oversees heritage sites, is Francesco Bandarin, a Venetian who now serves as UNESCO's assistant director-general for culture.

J) Earlier this year, Italy signed an accord with UNESCO to establish a task force of police art detectives and archaeologists(考古学家) to protect cultural heritage from natural disasters and terror groups, such as ISIS. The accord underlined Italy's global reputation as a good steward of art and culture.

K) But adding Venice to the UNESCO endangered list—which is dominated by sites in developing and conflict-ridden countries—would be an international embarrassment, and could even hurt Italy's profitable tourism industry. The Italian Culture Ministry says it is unaware of any government efforts to pressure UNESCO. As for the organization itself, it declined a request for an interview.

L) The city's current mayor, Luigi Brugnaro, has ridiculed UNESCO and told it to mind its own business, while continuing to support the cruise ship industry, which employs 5,000 Venice residents.

M) As for Venetians, they're beyond frustrated and hoping for a solution soon. "It's a nightmare for me. Some situations are really difficult with tourists around," says Giorgio as he navigates around a swelling crowd at the Rialto Bridge. "There are just so many of them. They never know where they are going, and do not walk in an orderly manner. Navigating the streets can be exhausting."

N) Then it hits him: This crowd isn't made up of tourists. They're Venetians. Giorgio says he's never experienced the Rialto Bridge this way in all his 22 years. "For once, we are the ones who are blocking the traffic," he says delightedly. "It feels unreal. It feels like we're some form of endangered species. It's just nice. The feeling is just pure." But, he worries, if tourism isn't managed and his fellow locals continue to move to the mainland, his generation might be the last who can call themselves native Venetians.

questions.stem: According to one study, what do green spaces do to people?
options: B) Add to their sustained happiness.
C) Help them build a positive attitude towards life.
D) Lessen their concerns about material well-being.
questions.passage:
Living in an urban area with green spaces has a long-lasting positive impact on people's mental well-being, a study has suggested. UK researchers found moving to a green space had a sustained positive effect, unlike pay rises or promotions, which only provided a short-term boost. Co-author Mathew White, from the University of Exeter, UK, explained that the study showed people living in greener urban areas were displaying fewer signs of depression or anxiety. "There could be a number of reasons," he said, "for example, people do many things to make themselves happier: they strive for promotion or pay rises, or they get married. But the trouble with those things is that within six months to a year, people are back to their original baseline levels of well-being. So, these things are not sustainable; they don't make us happy in the long term. We found that for some lottery (彩票) winners who had won more than £500,000 the positive effect was definitely there, but after six months to a year, they were back to the baseline."

Dr. White said his team wanted to see whether living in greener urban areas had a lasting positive effect on people's sense of well-being or whether the effect also disappeared after a period of time. To do this, the team used data from the British Household Panel Survey compiled by the University of Essex.

Explaining what the data revealed, he said: "What you see is that even after three years, mental health is still better, which is unlike many other things that we think will make us happy." He observed that people living in green spaces were less stressed, and less stressed people made more sensible decisions and communicated better.

With a growing body of evidence establishing a link between urban green spaces and a positive impact on human well-being, Dr. White said, "There's growing interest among public policy officials, but the trouble is who funds it. What we really need at a policy level is to decide where the money will come from to help support good quality local green spaces."
